# Intraabdominal abscesses

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Abdominal surgery > General abdominal surgery > Intraabdominal abscesses*

[Original Article Link](/library/8u0OG3)

---

## Summary

Intrabdominal <u>abscesses</u> (IAAs) are a relatively common manifestation of intrabdominal infections and can occur in almost any structure or compartment of the abdomen. Sources include infected intraabdominal organs, organ or <u>viscus</u> perforation, <u>surgical site infections</u>, and the spread of extraabdominal infections. Most IAAs present with nonspecific abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, and/or <u>sepsis</u>. Large <u>abscesses</u> may be palpable on examination, but imaging with abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> or CT abdomen is typically required for the diagnosis. Treatment includes <u>sepsis management</u>, <u>antibiotics</u>, rapid source control with <u>abscess</u> drainage, and treatment of the underlying disorder. IAAs > 3 cm in diameter generally require drainage. <u>Imaging-guided percutaneous drainage</u> is usually preferred, but surgical drainage may be necessary in some cases. The choice of <u>antibiotic</u> treatment depends on location and source of the <u>abscess</u> as well as other factors such as local resistance patterns. Management of the underlying disorder is often affected by the presence and extent of related <u>abscesses</u> and should be adjusted accordingly.

---

## Subphrenic abscess

* Definition: an accumulation of <u>pus</u> located directly under the <u>diaphragm</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Reported in ∼ 2% of patients post abdominal <u>surgery</u>

* No history of <u>surgery</u> in approx. 10% of patients

* Etiology: polymicrobial infection (e.g., due to <u>Enterococcus</u> spp., <u>E. coli</u>, and <u>Clostridium</u> spp.) following <u>intraperitoneal</u> perforation

* Most commonly a complication of <u>surgery</u> (e.g., <u>splenectomy</u>, <u>gastrectomy</u>) or secondary to conditions such as <u>diverticulitis</u>, <u>duodenal ulcers</u>, and <u>appendicitis</u>

* Trauma

* Pathophysiology: See “<u>Abscess</u>” for details.

* Clinical features: most commonly develop 3–6 weeks after inciting event

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Pain</u> over the 8<sup>th</sup>–11<sup>th</sup> <u>ribs</u> on the affected side

* <u>Cough</u>, increased <u>respiratory rate</u>, <u>pleural effusion</u>

* Diagnostics [[15]](/library/_Kc5QW0)

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u> can be used to visualize the <u>abscess</u>.

* <u>Chest x-ray</u> shows air below the <u>diaphragm</u>.

* Management: <u>abscess</u> drainage and <u>antibiotic</u> treatment (empiric, followed by tailored treatment according to <u>antibiogram</u>)

* Complications: <u>empyema</u>, <u>sepsis</u>

* Prognosis: high mortality (∼ 30%)

---

## Subhepatic abscess

* Definition: an accumulation of <u>pus</u> located below the <u>liver</u>

* Etiology

* <u>Cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Complication of cholecystectomy</u>

* Perforated <u>duodenal</u> or <u>gastric ulcer</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Vomiting</u>

* <u>Diffuse abdominal pain</u>

* <u>Abdominal rigidity</u>

* Diagnostics: well-demarcated, subhepatic, nonhomogeneous fluid density which may contain gas

* Management

* <u>Abscess</u> drainage and <u>antibiotic</u> treatment

* Treatment of the underlying cause

* See also “Treatment” in “<u>Pyogenic liver abscess</u>.”

---

## Splenic abscess

* Definition: an enclosed collection of <u>pus</u> within the <u>spleen</u> that is usually caused by hematogenous spread of bacteria from a <u>septic</u> source

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Uncommon in the general population  [[18]](/library/GmcBS10)

* Frequent in individuals with bacterial <u>endocarditis</u> (up to 30%)

* Associated with <u>immunocompromise</u> in up to 35% of cases (e.g., due to <u>HIV</u>/<u>AIDS</u>, <u>organ transplantation</u>, <u>malignancy</u>) [[17]](/library/smctS10)

* Pathophysiology

* Most common: predisposing factors such as <u>immunodeficiency</u>, <u>intravenous drug use</u>, trauma to the <u>spleen</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, and infectious conditions (especially <u>endocarditis</u>) → <u>bacteremia</u> and hematogenous spread → <u>splenic abscess</u>

* Infection of <u>splenic infarction</u> can also lead to a <u>splenic abscess</u>.

* Clinical features

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Left upper quadrant</u> <u>pain</u>, referred left shoulder <u>pain</u> (<u>Kehr sign</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Blood count: <u>leukocytosis</u>

* Chest <u>x-ray</u>: <u>left upper quadrant</u> mass, extraluminal air, <u>pleural effusion</u>, and elevated <u>diaphragm</u> on the left side

* CT: lesion with <u>hypodense</u> center and thick, heterogeneous rim

* Management

* Broad-spectrum <u>empirical antibiotic treatment</u> followed by tailored treatment after <u>blood culture</u> results are obtained

* <u>Gold standard</u>: <u>splenectomy</u>

* Alternative: CT/<u>ultrasound</u>-guided percutaneous drainage or surgical drainage
